For some time after their arrival they were occupied in the necessary work of rearing habitations to themselves amid the ruins of Jerusalem and its neighborhood. This preliminary work being completed, they addressed themselves to rebuild the altar of burnt offering. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4232"/><div sID="gen6147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4232"/><hi type="bold">3. they set the altar upon his bases--</hi>They reared it upon its old foundation, so that it occupied as nearly as possible the site on which it had formerly stood.<div eID="gen6147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they offered burnt offerings ... morning and evening--</hi>Deeming it their duty to perform the public rites of religion, they did not wait till the temple should be rebuilt and dedicated; but, at the outset, they resumed the daily service prescribed by the law (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Ex 29:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">Le 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.11">11</reference>), as well as observed the annual seasons of solemn observance. <div eID="gen6148" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4237"/><div sID="gen6153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4237"/><hi type="bold">12. But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers ... wept with a loud voice--</hi>Those painful emotions were excited by the sad contrast between the prosperous circumstances in which the foundations of the first temple had been laid and the desolate, reduced state of the country and city when the second was begun; between the inferior size and less costliness of the stones used in the foundations of the second (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.9">1Ki 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.10">10</reference>), and the much smaller extent of the foundation itself, including all the appurtenances of the building (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.3">Hag 2:3</reference>); between the comparative smallness of their present means and the immense resources of David and Solomon. Perhaps, however, the chief cause of grief was that the second temple would be destitute of those things which formed the great and distinguishing glory of the first; namely, the ark, the shekinah, the Urim and Thummim, &c. Not that this second temple was not a very grand and beautiful structure. But no matter how great its material splendor was, it was inferior in this respect to that of Solomon. Yet the glory of the second far outshone that of the first temple in another and more important point of view, namely, the receiving within its walls the incarnate Saviour (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen6153" type="x-p"/>
